---
title: "Pruning to a sparse model"
description: >
  Why rpf() prunes the forest's components, what it leaves out, the rules and
  the threshold, choosing them out of bag or by cross-validation, the display
  of three-way components, and prune = FALSE.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

A forest has many more components than the data have effects: every set of predictors that some tree splits on gives one, and with enough splits nearly every set does.
Most of them are tiny and fit noise.
By default `rpf()` prunes them, so that the model it returns has the few components worth reading, and predicts better.

```{r setup}
library(randomPlantedForest)
```

The data: two main effects, a two-way and a three-way interaction; `x5` has no effect.

```{r simulate}
make_data <- function(n) {
  d <- data.frame(matrix(runif(n * 5, -1, 1), ncol = 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:5))))
  d$y <- sin(pi * d$x1) + d$x2 + 2 * d$x1 * d$x3 + 3 * d$x2 * d$x3 * d$x4 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
  d
}
set.seed(3)
train <- make_data(1000)
test <- make_data(2000)
```

## The forest and the pruned model

`prune = FALSE` returns the forest itself.
`prune_components()` prunes a forest, and with its defaults it gives exactly the model that the default `rpf()` call returns from the same random number state:

```{r forest}
set.seed(10)
forest <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, prune = FALSE, nthreads = 2)
pruned <- prune_components(forest, train)

set.seed(10)
identical(predict(pruned, test), predict(rpf(y ~ ., data = train, nthreads = 2), test))
```

The pruned model does not hold the forest it was pruned from (`keep_forest = TRUE` keeps it, in `rpf()` and in `prune_components()`).
To try other settings, prune the forest again, as below.

The forest has `r sum(pruned$display$first$components$share > 0)` nonzero components; the pruned model keeps `r sum(pruned$components$kept)`:

```{r compare}
rmse <- function(m) sqrt(mean((test$y - predict(m, test)$.pred)^2))
c(forest = rmse(forest), pruned = rmse(pruned))
```

Often, the pruned model is both smaller and more accurate on new data.


## What is left out, and why

Every component `f_S` of the forest has a size: its share of the variance of the forest's prediction on the training rows, `Var(f_S) / Var(f)`.
A component is kept if its share is at least a threshold `tau`.
The forest's components, largest first (`pruned$display$first` is the model before the display step, below):

```{r shares}
first <- pruned$display$first
head(first$components[order(-first$components$share), c("component", "share", "kept")], 10)
```

Two rules are compared:

- **D** (drop): the prediction is the intercept plus the kept components, as the forest has them.
- **R** (drop and refit): one coefficient per kept component and a new intercept, fitted by least squares on the kept components.
  The components keep their shape and change their scale.
  This undoes the forest's shrinkage of interactions, which comes from averaging families of which some never find a given interaction.

The candidates are both rules at eight thresholds, `tau` = 0, 0.01%, 0.03%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 1%, 3% and 10%.

## The choice, out of bag

Each candidate is scored by its out-of-bag error: every family's components are evaluated at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample, so the score uses no refit of the forest.
The coefficients of rule R are fitted on these out-of-bag components too, because the forest's own components have fitted the noise of the training rows, and least squares on them would scale the components up.

The choice is the largest `tau` whose error is within one standard error of the lowest (`select = "1se"`), and at that `tau` the rule with the lower error:

```{r oob-table}
first$oob[, c("rule", "tau", "oob_rmse", "se_mse", "n_kept", "min", "one_se")]
```

```{r oob-plot, fig.alt = "Corrected out-of-bag error of rules D and R at each threshold tau, with the chosen candidate circled."}
tab <- first$oob
x <- seq_along(unique(tab$tau))
plot(NULL, xlim = range(x), ylim = range(tab$oob_rmse), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "tau", ylab = "corrected OOB RMSE")
axis(1, at = x, labels = format(unique(tab$tau), scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE),
     cex.axis = 0.8)
for (r in c("D", "R")) {
  s <- tab[tab$rule == r, ]
  lines(x, s$oob_rmse, type = "b", pch = 20, lty = if (r == "D") 2 else 1)
}
chosen <- tab[tab$one_se, ]
points(match(chosen$tau, unique(tab$tau)), chosen$oob_rmse, pch = 1, cex = 2, col = "orange", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("rule D", "rule R", "chosen"), lty = c(2, 1, NA), pch = c(20, 20, 1),
       col = c("black", "black", "orange"), bty = "n")
```

Here rule R's refit lowers the error far below rule D's at every threshold that keeps the four true components.
Under rule R the error changes little over a wide range of `tau`, so the 1-SE rule can take a large threshold and a small model.
`select = "min"` takes the lowest error instead, which keeps more small components.

Note that it can happen that pruning drops a small true component if its fitted signal is not strong enough.

## Other choices

`prune_components()` takes the candidates and the way of choosing as arguments.
A given rule and threshold are applied without a choice:

```{r given}
given <- prune_components(forest, train, rule = "D", tau = 0.01)
given$components$component[given$components$kept]
```

`select = "min"` takes the lowest out-of-bag error:

```{r min}
sum(prune_components(forest, train, select = "min")$components$kept)
```

`select_by = "cv"` scores the candidates by K-fold cross-validation instead, refitting the forest on each fold, so it costs K more fits.

Often out-of-bag and cross-validation choose the same rule and threshold, the former with lower cost, but not always.

```{r cv}
set.seed(10)
forest50 <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, n_families = 50, prune = FALSE, nthreads = 2)
by_cv <- prune_components(forest50, train, select_by = "cv", seed = 1)
by_cv$cv[by_cv$cv$one_se, c("rule", "tau", "cv_rmse", "n_kept")]
```

## The display: components of three predictors

A component of three predictors is shown as heat maps over two of them, one per interval of the third, and its own cut points can need hundreds of heat maps.
After the first pruning, every kept component of three or more predictors that needs more than `max_panels` (10) heat maps is coarsened:

- two of its predictors stay at full resolution;
- the others are cut into intervals with equal numbers of training rows, at most `max_panels` cells in all, and the component is averaged within each cell;
- of all such forms, the one that keeps most of the component's variance is taken.

Then the model is pruned again, by the same rule, with the coarsened components in place, so that the pruning judges the model that is shown and predicts.
Often this gives a slightly lower test error than coarsening after pruning, or not coarsening at all.

```{r display}
pruned$display$forms
```

`max_panels = Inf` (in `rpf()` or `prune_components()`) skips this step, and [Reading the model](reading-the-model.html) shows how to read a coarsened component.

## The forest itself: `prune = FALSE`

With `prune = FALSE`, `rpf()` returns the forest, of class `rpf`.
Its `predict_components()` gives every component, after purifying the forest on first use:

```{r all-components}
ncol(predict_components(forest, test)$m)
```

This is the place to start for your own pruning rule, or to look at components that the default leaves out.
